title: Why 'Good Enough' Decision-Makers End Up Happier
alt_title_1: Herbert Simon & Barry Schwartz on Satisficing vs Maximizing
alt_title_2: Stop Over-Researching Small Choices: The 10-Minute Satisfice Rule
description_hook: Nobel laureate Herbert Simon coined 'satisficing' in 1956, and psychologist Barry Schwartz proved in a 2002 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology study that relentless maximizers feel worse even after winning objectively good outcomes. Here is when 'good enough' wins.

affiliate_cta.offer_name: Reversible vs Irreversible Decision Filter + Reading List
affiliate_cta.pinned_comment: What minor purchase or choice recently stole way too many browser tabs from your week? Grab our Reversible Decision Filter + book list here: https://kenvh0010-lang.github.io/admin/bio/

scenes.headline: Why 50 Open Browser Tabs Leave You Less Happy
bullets: Four hours spent comparing nearly identical options
Less satisfaction after buying than fast deciders
scenes.narration: Why do people who spend four hours comparing fifty nearly identical hotels end up less happy than decisive travelers who pick in five minutes?
scenes.source: Barry Schwartz et al., Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2002)

scenes.headline: Herbert Simon (1956) & Barry Schwartz (2002)
bullets: Simon (1956): 'satisfice' = pick first option meeting your bar
Schwartz et al. (2002): maximizers suffer chronic buyer's remorse
scenes.narration: Nobel laureate Herbert Simon coined satisficing in 1956 for choosing the first option that meets clear standards. In 2002, psychologist Barry Schwartz and colleagues proved relentless maximizers experience higher regret and lower satisfaction.
scenes.source: Herbert Simon, Psychological Review (1956); Schwartz et al., JPSP (2002)

scenes.headline: Spending Deep-Work Energy on Reversible Trivia
scenes.left_body: 3 hours researching $40 gear -> haunted by missed alternatives
scenes.right_body: 3 clear criteria + 10-min cap -> saves energy for big bets
scenes.narration: Maximizing reversible purchases drains hours of precious focus. Even after buying a top-rated laptop, maximizers torture themselves wondering whether tab forty-seven held a slightly better deal.

scenes.headline: Set 3 Criteria and a 10-Minute Timer
scenes.stat_label: FAST REVERSIBLE DECISIONS -> MORE CREATIVE BANDWIDTH
scenes.stat_subtext: Save deep research strictly for long-term asymmetric bets
scenes.narration: Reserve exhaustive research for rare, irreversible life bets. For everyday tools and purchases, define three must-have criteria, set a ten-minute timer, and pick the first match.

scenes.headline: Protect Bandwidth for Decisions That Compound
scenes.stat_label: DEFAULT SPEED LIMIT FOR REVERSIBLE CHOICES
bullets: Close comparison tabs once your baseline bar is met
Invest reclaimed hours into building durable skills and assets
scenes.narration: Satisfice small reversible choices quickly so your best mental energy stays locked on high-leverage work.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin decision rule based on Simon (1956) and Schwartz et al. (2002)
